sections.description: Walks through the patient’s timeline from preoperative heparin exposure through cardiac surgery, postoperative platelet trends, neurologic event, and initial management pivots, highlighting features that first raised concern for HIT/aHIT.
subtopics: Preoperative context: transradial catheterization with 2000 U UFH while on apixaban; scheduled cardiac surgery one week later
Intraoperative course: CPB with 45,000 U UFH; uneventful surgery and hemodynamic stability
Postoperative thromboprophylaxis: dalteparin (LMWH) POD1–4; switch to prophylactic fondaparinux on POD5
Platelet kinetics after CPB: expected early drop vs observed progressive fall to 50×10^9/L by POD5 and nadir 13×10^9/L
Neurologic deterioration: delirium prompting CT; acute left parietal infarct on POD6
Initial labs: stable hemoglobin, normal WBC, no hemolysis, elevated fibrinogen (acute phase), normal PT/PTT; peripheral smear without schistocytes early
Early suspicion of HIT in cardiac surgery: how the timing and severity deviated from typical post-CPB thrombocytopenia

sections.section_title: Mechanisms and Phenotypes: Classic HIT versus Autoimmune HIT (aHIT)
sections.description: Explains the immunopathogenesis of HIT and the distinctive features of aHIT that account for this patient’s severe and atypical course, including the unique laboratory activation profile.
subtopics: Classic HIT immunobiology: PF4/heparin complexes, IgG immune complexes, FcγRIIa-mediated platelet activation, prothrombotic state
Why cardiac surgery is high risk: PF4 release, inflammation, CPB-induced platelet activation, postoperative heparin exposure
Autoimmune HIT (aHIT): heparin-independent PF4-reactive antibodies that can activate platelets without heparin; typically more severe, persistent thrombocytopenia; higher thrombotic risk
Early-onset HIT mechanism: anamnestic response from preoperative UFH exposure causing platelet fall before POD5
Assay principles: PF4/polyanion ELISA (high OD indicates strong antibody burden) vs functional SRA (heparin-dependent activation profile)

This case’s serology: strong ELISA (OD 2.2); SRA with robust activation at 0, 0.1, 0.3 U/mL heparin and inhibition at 100 U/mL; partial resistance to FcγRIIa blockade by IV.3—an unusually severe aHIT phenotype
Evolution of antibody phenotype over time: waning heparin-independent activity with later SRA shifting toward heparin dependence

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Reasoning in Early Post-Cardiac Surgery Thrombocytopenia
sections.description: Outlines a structured approach to evaluating thrombocytopenia after CPB, shows how alternative causes were excluded, and details why HIT/aHIT became the leading diagnosis despite an atypical SRA report.
subtopics: Frameworks: expected CPB-related thrombocytopenia vs biphasic fall suggestive of HIT; utility and limitations of the 4Ts score post-cardiac surgery
Differential diagnosis: infection/sepsis, DIC, cardiogenic shock, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia, post-transfusion purpura, surgery-associated TTP, ongoing bleeding/consumption

Data synthesis in this patient: normal hemodynamics, negative cultures, no transfusions, normal haptoglobin early, initial smear without schistocytes, stable hemoglobin—argues against competing diagnoses
Linking timing to exposure: identifying preoperative UFH at catheterization as the sensitizing event

Interpreting the laboratories: strong PF4 ELISA supporting immune HIT; understanding an ‘indeterminate’ SRA when findings actually signal aHIT (heparin-independent activation and partial Fc-blockade resistance)
Role of repeat/serial functional testing and correlation with clinical course
Imaging confirmation of thrombotic complication: ischemic stroke consistent with HIT prothrombotic risk

sections.section_title: Management of Severe aHIT with Arterial Thrombosis
sections.description: Details immediate and longitudinal treatment decisions, including non-heparin anticoagulation strategy, adjunctive IVIG, biomarker monitoring for hypercoagulability, and rationale for therapy adjustments.
subtopics: Immediate steps: stop all heparin/LMWH; avoid platelet transfusions unless life-threatening bleeding
Choice of non-heparin anticoagulant: rationale for argatroban initiation (short half-life, titratable in setting of stroke and profound thrombocytopenia); dosing and aPTT targets
Adjunctive high-dose IVIG in aHIT: mechanism (FcγRIIa saturation and immune modulation), dosing strategy, expected brisk platelet rise vs attenuated response seen here
Monitoring hypercoagulability and treatment adequacy: trends in fibrinogen (consumptive decline), d-dimer (peaks), and smear schistocytes
Therapeutic pivot: switch to fondaparinux due to concern for persistent hypercoagulability; dosing, once-daily convenience, and rationale
Antithrombin dependence of fondaparinux: assessment of antithrombin level, reason for AT concentrate supplementation
Stroke considerations: balancing anticoagulation intensity with hemorrhagic transformation risk; preference for agents with predictable reversal/offset
Duration and transition: continuation until platelet recovery and clinical stabilization; eventual return to apixaban for long-term AF management

sections.description: Summarizes clinical recovery and evolving serology, then distills practical takeaways for recognizing and treating aHIT in cardiac surgery patients.
subtopics: Outcome: gradual platelet recovery to normal by POD62; full neurological recovery
Serial functional testing: persistence of strong SRA activation for months; later shift toward heparin-dependent profile as aHIT antibodies waned
Long-term anticoagulation plan: discontinuation of fondaparinux, resumption of apixaban; future heparin avoidance and documentation/alerts
Key clinical pearls: early-onset HIT after cardiac surgery usually reflects preoperative heparin; aHIT often presents with severe thrombocytopenia and consumptive markers
Laboratory nuance: strong ELISA plus heparin-independent SRA activation and incomplete FcγRIIa blockade indicate aHIT—even if initially labeled ‘indeterminate’
Therapeutic insights: consider IVIG early in severe aHIT but anticipate variable response; monitor coagulation biomarkers; be prepared to switch anticoagulants if hypercoagulability persists
When to involve specialists and reference labs: hematology consultation and expert functional testing to guide complex cases
